blind.location: Printed p. 84 (source page 6), Problem 2
blind.quote:
Problem 2. Alice typically scores around 80 on weekly 100-point quizzes in one
     of her classes. One week she sets a goal of scoring 90. She scores 87.
       Betty typically scores around 80 on weekly 100-point quizzes in one of her classes.
     One week she decides to do her best. She scores 83.
       Overall, who will be more satisfied with her performance? [N ⫽ 60]

   Both Alice and Betty typically perform at the same level on their weekly
quizzes, and this week both have exceeded their typical score. Thus if they
used their normal performance as their reference point, both should be happy
but Alice should be happier. However, because goals operate as reference
points, Alice ends up in the domain of losses because she performs three
points below her reference point. Although Alice performs above Betty in
absolute terms, people agree that she will be less satisfied with her perfor-
mance ( p ⬍ .05 by χ 2 ).

At 42 sit-ups, the slopes of the two value functions indicate that Charles
receives lower benefits from an additional sit-up than David. Note that

to his goal and experiencing smaller effects of diminishing sensitivity, to
exert more effort after the 42nd sit-up (p ⬍ .05 by χ 2 ).

blind.location: Printed p. 90 (source page 12), Problem 7
blind.quote:
Problem 7 successfully distinguishes the value function approach from
the traditional goal-setting approach. When Charles and David are both be-
low their goals, the value function in Fig. 2 clearly predicts that Charles will
exert more effort than David at 28 sit-ups because he receives higher benefits.
Again, this prediction follows from diminishing sensitivity, Charles is closer
to his goal and is much more sensitive to movements toward it, b′30 (28) ⫽
v′(⫺2) ⬎ v′(⫺12) ⫽ b′40 (28). Consistent with the value function prediction
but not goal setting, participants expected Charles to exert more effort after
the 28th sit-up (p ⬍ .001 by χ 2 ).

blind.location: Printed p. 91 (source page 13), Problem 8
blind.quote:
Problem 8. [N ⫽ 47] Jim decides that he would like to donate more time to charity.
    His schedule won’t permit more than 4 h per week, so he sets a personal goal of
    working 40 h over the next 10 weeks at a neighborhood soup kitchen. Soon after
    starting, Jim learns that the soup kitchen will be forced to close in 4 weeks.
       Kyle decides that he would like to donate more time to charity. His schedule
    won’t permit more than 4 h per week, so he sets a personal goal of working 200 h
    over the next year at a neighborhood soup kitchen. Soon after starting, Kyle learns
    that the soup kitchen will be forced to close in 4 weeks.
       Who will donate more time to the soup kitchen over the next 4 weeks?
       Please circle one Jim (81%) Kyle (19%)

   Note that Jim and Kyle have set goals that require them to work at a
similar rate (4 h per week). Also note that neither will reach his goal before
the soup kitchen closes. However, according to the value function, Jim feels
that he is making more progress than Kyle: b40 (16) ⫽ v(⫺24) ⫺ v(⫺40) ⬎
v(⫺184) ⫺ v(⫺200) ⫽ b200 (16). Consistent with the notion of a ‘‘starting
problem,’’ people feel that Kyle will find it more difficult to start working
toward his high goal.

disposition.reason: Problem 8 gives Jim 81%, Kyle 19%, and a qualitative starting-problem interpretation; no numeric test statistic or p value is printed.

worker_notes:
Original side is an unassigned placeholder, not an assessment of original-source availability. Every assigned row has a blank description; study 1 and a page locator do not distinguish the critical predictor/outcome/test. Candidate common model N is documented directly, not derived: 2968 students; 882 teachers; 480 schools. No arithmetic performed. Continuous-variable standardisation is explicitly documented on p. 7: We standardized all continuous variables in the analysis (M = 0, SD = 1). This does not establish that every categorical coefficient is a fully standardised beta. Page 8 reading narrative candidate coefficient/p pairs (same-test pairs, not assigned): reading methods-course school average gamma500=-0.30, p=0.04; school SES gamma700=0.03, p=0.05; prior achievement beta100=0.74, p<.001; elapsed time beta200=0.10, p<.001; student SES beta300=0.04, p=.006; gender beta500=0.12, p<.001. Page 8 Table 3 also contains school/teacher/student random variances (.06/.08/.87 for reading; .01/.11/.88 for mathematics), ICCs and reliability estimates; these are distinct metrics and tests. Page 9 mathematics narrative candidate coefficient/p pairs (same-test pairs, not assigned): beta100=0.76, p<.001; beta200=0.06, p<.001; beta300=0.05, p=.004; beta500=-0.15, p<.001. The narrative labels beta100 previous reading achievement but its interpretation and Table 4 identify prior mathematics achievement; retain this source inconsistency. Table 4 pp. 9–10 provides multiple school-, teacher-, and student-level estimates for both outcomes with SEs and a p<.05 star legend, rather than exact p for every coefficient. blind.quote: As predicted, the postextinction administration of l -DOPA compared to placebo (see Fig. 1a ) enhanced extinction memory retrieval and reduced the expression of fear at test on day 3 (stimulus: F 1,33 = 44.61, P < .001, partial η 2 = 0.58, stimulus × group: F 1,33 = 6.58, P = 0.02, partial η 2 = 0.17; n = 35; Fig. 1b ). ... g The postextinction administration of l -DOPA had a significant positive effect on number of potential CS+ offset-related vmPFC reactivations (path a: ß = 0.97, SE = 0.30, T 33 = 3.23, P = 0.003; n = 35). The number of potential CS+ offset-related vmPFC reactivations 45 min after extinction was significantly negatively related to smaller differential CRs at test on day 3 (path b: β = −0.10, SE = 0.03, T 33 = −4.26, P = 0.0002; n = 35). After inclusion of number of potential CS+ offset-related vmPFC reactivations into the latter model, the significant effect of drug on CRs at test (path c: ß = −0.15, SE = 0.06, T 33 = −2.57, P = 0.02; n = 35) decreased (path c’: β = −0.06, SE = 0.06, T 32 = −0.98, P = 0.33; n = 35), indicating that the effect of l -DOPA on CRs at test on day 3 was significantly mediated (c–c’ = −0.09, 95% CI: −0.13 to −0.02, P = 0.007; bootstrapping procedure with 10,000 simulations; n = 35) by number of potential CS+ offset-related vmPFC reactivations 45 min after extinction ... Intriguingly, the number of reactivations of the CS+ offset-related vmPFC pattern at 45 min postextinction mediated the effect of l -DOPA on CRs at test (Fig. 2g ; mediation analysis—indirect mediator effect: β = −0.09, 95% CI: −0.13 to −0.02, P = 0.007; bootstrapping procedure with 10,000 simulations; n = 35).

blind.location: p.266, pairwise contrast results beneath Table 3
blind.quote:
In phase 0, the control group rated bad items
significantly lower than the intervention group, estimated difference = −0.261, 95%
CI = [−0.456, −0.0653], p = .009. Nevertheless, in phase 1 the control group rated bad items
significantly higher than the intervention group, estimated difference = 0.525, 95% CI = [0.328,
0.722], p < .0001, and phase 2, estimated difference = 0.543, 95% CI = [0.349, 0.7362], p < .0001.
The third column in Table 3 shows the model parameters for predictors group by phase on
knowledge application ratings for each good quality item as a dependent variable. There were no
significant differences between groups for the good items in phase 0 or in phase 2, ps > .05; but
in phase 1 the control group rated good items significantly lower than the intervention group,
estimated difference = −0.2589, 95% CI = [−0.448, −0.07], p = .0073. There were no significant
differences between the ratings in each phase in the control group or in the intervention group,
ps > .05.

blind.location: p.274 Discussion and RQ1 discussion
blind.quote:
Our results are in line with those from the
original study (Pérez et al., 2018). Overall, evidence shows that the intervention improved college
students’ sourcing skills in tasks where they explicitly had to use source information to make decisions
and that the effects lasted to the delayed post-test. Moreover, the results from a novel, ecological task,
a final term team essay with no prompts to use reliable sources, suggest that the intervention also had
effects on naturalistic college online inquiry behavior. ... Our preregistered hypotheses were supported by the data: After the intervention, trained students
became specifically more critical of bad quality websites than the control group, even when the latter
initially outperformed them, and this difference persisted to the delayed post-test.

differences between the ratings in each phase in the control group or in the intervention group,
ps > .05.

blind.location: p.274 Discussion and RQ1 discussion
blind.quote:
Our results are in line with those from the
original study (Pérez et al., 2018). Overall, evidence shows that the intervention improved college
students’ sourcing skills in tasks where they explicitly had to use source information to make decisions
and that the effects lasted to the delayed post-test. Moreover, the results from a novel, ecological task,
a final term team essay with no prompts to use reliable sources, suggest that the intervention also had
effects on naturalistic college online inquiry behavior. ... Our preregistered hypotheses were supported by the data: After the intervention, trained students
became specifically more critical of bad quality websites than the control group, even when the latter
initially outperformed them, and this difference persisted to the delayed post-test.

blind.location: p.274 Discussion and RQ1 discussion
blind.quote:
Our results are in line with those from the
original study (Pérez et al., 2018). Overall, evidence shows that the intervention improved college
students’ sourcing skills in tasks where they explicitly had to use source information to make decisions
and that the effects lasted to the delayed post-test. Moreover, the results from a novel, ecological task,
a final term team essay with no prompts to use reliable sources, suggest that the intervention also had
effects on naturalistic college online inquiry behavior. ... Our preregistered hypotheses were supported by the data: After the intervention, trained students
became specifically more critical of bad quality websites than the control group, even when the latter
initially outperformed them, and this difference persisted to the delayed post-test.

blind.location: p.274 Discussion and RQ1 discussion
blind.quote:
Our results are in line with those from the
original study (Pérez et al., 2018). Overall, evidence shows that the intervention improved college
students’ sourcing skills in tasks where they explicitly had to use source information to make decisions
and that the effects lasted to the delayed post-test. Moreover, the results from a novel, ecological task,
a final term team essay with no prompts to use reliable sources, suggest that the intervention also had
effects on naturalistic college online inquiry behavior. ... Our preregistered hypotheses were supported by the data: After the intervention, trained students
became specifically more critical of bad quality websites than the control group, even when the latter
initially outperformed them, and this difference persisted to the delayed post-test.

disposition.reason: Authors give a positive paper-level verdict (candidate vocabulary successful) and state RQ1 preregistered hypotheses were supported. This does not establish an outcome/phase-specific verdict for an unidentified assigned effect; good/bad item and phase patterns differ. Retain narrative as candidate, with no row-specific classification.

blind.sample_role: Unresolved analytic count of morpheme contexts/annotations for the chi-square test; not the contributor count of 40 learner texts.
blind.exclusions: 127 eligible contributors were narrowed to 40 texts on word count; all four proficiency groups contribute. No critical-test contingency counts or explicit analytic-N/exclusion statement are supplied. Obligatory contexts and non-obligatory oversuppliance annotations are distinguished in the methods.
blind.location: p.23 Figure 4; pp.24,30–31; pp.41–42 group score method; p.17 Table 2
blind.quote:
Raw frequencies of annotations ... 46 ... ing ... Figure 4. Annotation statistics for the current study. ... Figure 4 shows the statistics of all text files for the number of annotations made for each
morpheme out of a total number of 1197 annotations.

disposition.reason: Named progressive -ing comparison located in Table 4. Figure 4 prints 46 annotations for this morpheme, but Table 4 does not state analytic N or contingency-cell counts. The methods distinguish obligatory contexts used in TLU-rate denominators from non-obligatory oversuppliance tags. Certification of all annotations as the critical-test N would require an unsupported denominator assumption. The 40 learner texts are contributors, not this test’s context-level analytic N.
disposition.location: p.23 Figure 4; p.24 TLU definition; pp.30–31 section 4.2.1/Table 4; pp.41–42 group score method
disposition.quote:
Raw frequencies of annotations ... 46 ... ing ... Figure 4. Annotation statistics for the current study. ... Figure 4 shows the statistics of all text files for the number of annotations made for each
morpheme out of a total number of 1197 annotations. ... TLU rates were calculated by dividing the suppliance in obligatory context (SOC) with
obligatory context (OC), in other words the accuracy of using the morpheme in question. ... Group score method: the TLU counts are summed and divided by the total OC of all
       learners in the sample. (this was used in the reference study and current study)
disposition.calculation: No calculation. Candidate annotation count = 46; contributor sample = 40 texts. Neither is asserted as critical-test analytic N; no df-based derivation or sum.

worker_target_description: Kontkanen (2024), section 4.2.1 and Table 4 current-study ing column: chi-square comparison of progressive -ing TLU rates between beginners (A1+A2) and intermediates (B1+B2). Matching is based on the named morpheme and comparison, not numeric values.
worker_notes: Only n_r and reported_success were assigned; original, replication es and replication p are unassigned null placeholders. Figure 4 explicitly labels 46 as the total number of progressive -ing annotations. This is retained as a candidate, not certified as Table 4 analytic N. The study distinguishes OC from NOC/oversuppliance (pp.19–20), defines TLU rate as SOC/OC (p.24), and uses the group score method across all learners (pp.41–42). Table 4 supplies chi-square and p values without N or underlying contingency cells. Forty texts are contributor units and are not substituted for morpheme-context observations. No N sum or effect-size conversion was performed. The authors describe study-level disagreement with the reference study (p.44), and significance patterns (p.30), but do not label replication success for this particular Table 4 comparison. No per-effect verdict is inferred from matching significance or from conclusions about acquisition ranks or error subtypes. Rendered PDF pp.23 and 31 were inspected for Figure 4 and Table 4 layout.

input.description: Article. The annotation covers OCs of (in)definite articles (a(n)/the). Given that the ‘zero article’ was disregarded in previous MOS, it was also disregarded here for comparative purposes. The non-suppliance of an article in an (in)definite OC was tagged as omission. Also, given that both definite and indefinite articles were analysed as a single morpheme in previous MOS, we analysed them similarly, even if we are aware that they are better analysed separately as they do not emerge simultaneously (cf. the discussion in Section 4.4). Selection of one article for the other was tagged as ‘mis-selection’. The forms a/an were understood as spelling variants, so selection of one when the other was expected was not tagged as NTLU. Importantly, determining the OC of the/a(n) is based on information-status distinctions deriving from discourse, i.e., on whether the entity has been previously mentioned in the discourse (i.e., discourse-old, topic) or not (i.e., discourse-new, focus), and therefore whether or not the referent is known to the reader. Articles were annotated independently of the appearance of characters in the picture story, which could give the sense of old information, but technically introduce discoursenew information when retelling the story to a reader. Therefore, ILA considers hearer/reader knowledge (and not speaker knowledge) to determine discourse-old/discourse-new distinctions (cf. Hawkins, 2001).

worker_target_description: Original Finnish nested case-control study; several candidate exposure contrasts on p. 5, row-specific test unresolved.
worker_notes: All four assigned rows have identical study, description, and p. 5 locator. Table 2 printed adjusted OR candidates (all versus <1 year of the corresponding exposure): prolactin-increasing 1–4 years 1·04 (95% CI 0·79–1·36), ≥5 years 1·56 (1·27–1·92); prolactin-sparing 1–4 years 0·95 (0·73–1·25), ≥5 years 1·19 (0·90–1·58). Results on this page additionally report cumulative ≥5000 DDD adjusted OR 1·36 (1·09–1·70) for prolactin-increasing and 1·15 (0·84–1·58) for prolactin-sparing exposure; cancer-subtype ≥5-year adjusted OR candidates are 2·36 (lobular) and 1·42 (ductal). Source title and DOI match the assigned original primary paper. PDF p. 5 rendered and visually inspected. Replication and reported_success are unassigned placeholders.

disposition.quote:
Our final samples of 1,479 people for testing H1 and 2,697
people for the remaining analyses ... The contrast of interest (generic-
masculine vs. internal-I and feminine-masculine form) also reached significance (t(1473) = 15.4, p <
.001 d = 0.84). Additionally, its 90% confidence interval (90% CId [0.75, 0.93]) fell outside of our
equivalence bounds of Δd = ± 0.18, leading us to reject the hypothesis that the effect of the generic
masculine vs. alternatives is equivalent to zero. Taken together, this can be viewed as evidence that
people on average listed more women when gender-inclusive alternatives were used compared to the
generic masculine. Therefore, we replicated the effect of Stahlberg et al. (2001). ... GM vs. II       0.49    0.02   -23.01     < .001
GM vs. FM       0.71    0.02   -11.04     < .001
GM vs. G*       0.64

people for the remaining analyses ... The contrast of interest (generic-
masculine vs. internal-I and feminine-masculine form) also reached significance (t(1473) = 15.4, p <
.001 d = 0.84). Additionally, its 90% confidence interval (90% CId [0.75, 0.93]) fell outside of our
equivalence bounds of Δd = ± 0.18, leading us to reject the hypothesis that the effect of the generic
masculine vs. alternatives is equivalent to zero. Taken together, this can be viewed as evidence that
people on average listed more women when gender-inclusive alternatives were used compared to the
generic masculine. Therefore, we replicated the effect of Stahlberg et al. (2001). ... GM vs. II       0.49    0.02   -23.01     < .001
GM vs. FM       0.71    0.02   -11.04     < .001
GM vs. G*       0.64

disposition.location: pp.8–9 pre-study/H1 hypotheses; p.19 final samples; pp.21–25 H1/H2 results
disposition.quote:
Our final samples of 1,479 people for testing H1 and 2,697
people for the remaining analyses ... The contrast of interest (generic-
masculine vs. internal-I and feminine-masculine form) also reached significance (t(1473) = 15.4, p <
.001 d = 0.84). Additionally, its 90% confidence interval (90% CId [0.75, 0.93]) fell outside of our
equivalence bounds of Δd = ± 0.18, leading us to reject the hypothesis that the effect of the generic
masculine vs. alternatives is equivalent to zero. Taken together, this can be viewed as evidence that
people on average listed more women when gender-inclusive alternatives were used compared to the
generic masculine. Therefore, we replicated the effect of Stahlberg et al. (2001). ... GM vs. II       0.49    0.02   -23.01     < .001
GM vs. FM       0.71    0.02   -11.04     < .001
GM vs. G*       0.64

Experiment 1 candidate test A: main effect of trial number on the three metamemory ratings, F (1, 76) = 27.00, p < .001, printed partial eta squared 0.26. Candidate test B: main effect of check number on those ratings, F (1, 76) = 0.90, p = .765, printed partial eta squared 0.001. Preserve this printed F/p pair without correction. disposition.reason: The description identifies the broad training relationship and senior-officer sample but does not specify the dependent variable, model term (Time, Group, or interaction), pre/post exploratory comparison, or group-specific contrast. Multiple primary tests fit. Page-only locators in an unpaginated HTML parse do not uniquely identify a test. No assignments are made from audit_id, row order, requested metric, or numeric agreement. All positive values remain unassigned candidates; analytic n is also unresolved because outcome/model and group-specific analysis determine the participant subset. No N is derived from df and no metric is converted. Printed candidates include inequalities such as partial eta squared <0.01 and p<0.001, retained literally in the quoted blocks. Even where the authors call p<.05 main effects non-significant, printed p values are preserved without reinterpretation. Explicit candidate participant Ns: Hit Factor 43 (21 control/22 intervention); Response Time 38 (21/17); First Hit 25 (13/12); Muzzle Position 24 (12/12); Closed Eye(s) 6 (5/1). These are model/outcome-specific, not a universally applicable N. Group-specific contrasts also exist. Recruitment N=45 is not substituted.

Multiple primary tests fit. Page-only locators in an unpaginated HTML parse do not uniquely identify a test. No assignments are made from audit_id, row order, requested metric, or numeric agreement. All positive values remain unassigned candidates; analytic n is also unresolved because outcome/model and group-specific analysis determine the participant subset. No N is derived from df and no metric is converted. Printed candidates include inequalities such as partial eta squared <0.01 and p<0.001, retained literally in the quoted blocks. disposition.reason: The description identifies the broad training relationship and senior-officer sample but does not specify the dependent variable, model term (Time, Group, or interaction), pre/post exploratory comparison, or group-specific contrast. Multiple primary tests fit. Page-only locators in an unpaginated HTML parse do not uniquely identify a test. No assignments are made from audit_id, row order, requested metric, or numeric agreement. All positive values remain unassigned candidates; analytic n is also unresolved because outcome/model and group-specific analysis determine the participant subset. No N is derived from df and no metric is converted. Printed candidates include inequalities such as partial eta squared <0.01 and p<0.001, retained literally in the quoted blocks. Even where the authors call p<.05 main effects non-significant, printed p values are preserved without reinterpretation. Explicit candidate participant Ns: Hit Factor 43 (21 control/22 intervention); Response Time 38 (21/17); First Hit 25 (13/12); Muzzle Position 24 (12/12); Closed Eye(s) 6 (5/1). These are model/outcome-specific, not a universally applicable N. Group-specific contrasts also exist. Recruitment N=45 is not substituted.

these ﬁndings to be in support of the BBS hypothesis and the original ﬁndings.

disposition.quote:
We conducted a series of one-tailed paired samples t-tests, and found that participants
showed a general tendency to view themselves as less susceptible to biases across the three
samples (Study 1a: M d = –0.75, t(44) = –4.54, p <.001, dz = –0.68, 95% CI [–1.01, –0.35];
Study 2: M d = –1.15; t(302) = –16.16, p < .001; dz = –0.93, 95% CI [–1.06, –0.79]; Study
3: M d = –1.80; t(620) = –32.04, p <.001, dz = –1.29, 95% CI [–1.39, –1.18]). We conclude
these ﬁndings to be in support of the BBS hypothesis and the original ﬁndings.

Studies 1a and 1b were meant as a pre-test of the eﬀects in an undergraduate class
covering topics of open science and social psychology, and were designed to replicate the
bias blind spot (BBS) eﬀect (Study 1 Survey 2) and the better than average eﬀect (BAE)
(Study 2), reported in the target study. ... A total of 310 American Amazon Mechanical Turk (MTurk) participants completed the study
using TurkPrime.com (Litman et al., 2017). Of those, seven participants were excluded
based on pre-registered exclusion criteria1, leaving 303 participants included in the analysis ... We conducted one-sample one-tailed t-tests and found that participants rated themselves as
having personality characteristics that are more positive (Study 1b: M = 5.74, t(42) = 5.09,
p < .001, dz = 0.78, 95% CI [0.43, 1.11]; Study 3: M = 6.42; t(620) = 31.74, p < .001; dz =
1.27, 95% CI [1.17, 1.38]) and less negative (Study 1b: M = 4.16, t(42) = –4.55, p < .001,
dz = –0.69, 95% CI [–1.02, –0.36]; Study 3: M = 3.21; t (620) = –30.38, p <.001; dz =
–1.22, 95% CI [–1.32, –1.11]) than others’. We conclude support of the better than average
eﬀect.

disposition.quote:
Studies 1a and 1b were meant as a pre-test of the eﬀects in an undergraduate class
covering topics of open science and social psychology, and were designed to replicate the
bias blind spot (BBS) eﬀect (Study 1 Survey 2) and the better than average eﬀect (BAE)
(Study 2), reported in the target study. ... We conducted a series of one-tailed paired samples t-tests, and found that participants
showed a general tendency to view themselves as less susceptible to biases across the three
samples (Study 1a: M d = –0.75, t(44) = –4.54, p <.001, dz = –0.68, 95% CI [–1.01, –0.35];
Study 2: M d = –1.15; t(302) = –16.16, p < .001; dz = –0.93, 95% CI [–1.06, –0.79]; Study
3: M d = –1.80; t(620) = –32.04, p <.001, dz = –1.29, 95% CI [–1.39, –1.18]). We conclude
these ﬁndings to be in support of the BBS hypothesis and the original ﬁndings. ... We conducted one-sample one-tailed t-tests and found that participants rated themselves as
having personality characteristics that are more positive (Study 1b: M = 5.74, t(42) = 5.09,
p < .001, dz = 0.78, 95% CI [0.43, 1.11]; Study 3: M = 6.42; t(620) = 31.74, p < .001; dz =
1.27, 95% CI [1.17, 1.38]) and less negative (Study 1b: M = 4.16, t(42) = –4.55, p < .001,
dz = –0.69, 95% CI [–1.02, –0.36]; Study 3: M = 3.21; t (620) = –30.38, p <.001; dz =
–1.22, 95% CI [–1.32, –1.11]) than others’. We conclude support of the better than average
eﬀect.

disposition.quote:
Response times were collected at different trial stages (hand movement initiation,

object contact, and object collection) using C#/.NET code embedded into the VR

application. Kolmogorov-Smirnov tests for normality of median response times (RTs)

signaled normal distribution of the data (zs < .98, ps > .29) and RTs for movement onset

and object contact were subjected to separate 2 x 2 repeated measures ANOVAs

comprising the factors OBJECTfood,ball and INTERACTIONgrasp,ward. Median collection times,

available for grasp trials only, were subjected to a paired t-test. ... One male participant was not comfortable with the hand tracking procedure and

repeatedly failed in positioning the starting hand. Two female participant’s data were lost

due to technical problems. Data are reported for the remaining 20 participants.

Median response times after object

onset were submitted to the 2 x 2 repeated measures ANOVA comprising the factors

two-way interaction was significant, F(1,19)=0.13, p=.72. ... Ward movements were executed faster than grasp movements (Mean difference:

218.72 ms, SE=60.88 ms) as reflected by a significant main effect of

INTERACTIONgrasp,ward, F(1,19)=12.90, p=.002, ηp²=0.41. Again, a timely advantage

emerged for Food objects, F(1,19)=4.50, p=.05, ηp²=0.19, but there was no significant

two-way interaction effect, F(1,19)=1.19, p=.29.

disposition.location: Manuscript pp.26–28, §3.3.1 (accuracy and references to source in justifications)
disposition.quote:
The

model demonstrated a significant main effect of group, χ² (1) = 10.68, p < .01, with more

correct responses in the trained (M = 0.72, SE ... = 0.15; OR = 0.39, CI 0.23-0.64); and phase, χ² (2) = 8.13, p < .05, with more correct

responses in the post-test 1 (M = 0.65, SE = 0.20) and post-test 2 (M = 0.71, SE = 0.21) than

in the pre-test (M = 0.52, SE = 0.19; OR = 0.52, CI 0.27-0.99 and OR = 0.42, CI 0.22-0.82 for

the post-test 1 and post-test 2, respectively). More importantly, the interaction between these

two factors was also significant, χ² (2) = 9.73, p < .01 (see Figure 4). Post-hoc comparisons

showed no group differences in the pre-test phase, χ² (1) = 0.0001, p ≃ 1.00 (OR = 0.99, CI

0.34-2.95); whereas the trained group outperformed the control group in the post-test 1, χ² (1)

= 14.90, p < .001 (OR = 0.19, CI 0.05-0.64), and post-test 2, χ² (1) = 7.19, p < .05 (OR = 0.31,

CI 0.09-1.08). Therefore, consistent with our hypothesis, trained students were better than

controls at detecting more reliable source information after the intervention. Importantly, this

finding was also true three weeks later, indicating the intervention had a rather robust impact. ... References to source in ... the post-test 1 (M = 0.47, SE = 0.17) and post-test 2 (M = 0.47, SE = 0.17) compared to the

pre-test (M = 0.24, SE = 0.19; OR = 0.33, CI 0.20-0.55 and OR = 0.34, CI 0.20-0.57 for the

post-test 1 and post-test 2, respectively); and condition, χ² (1) = 24.53, p < .001, with less

source reference to the less reliable (M = 0.29, SE = 0.16) compared to the more reliable

source (M = 0.49, SE = 0.15; OR = 2.48, CI 1.75-3.51).

      Importantly, the three two-way interactions were also significant. Post-hoc comparisons

in the interaction of group and phase, χ² (2) = 15.67, p < .001, demonstrated that trained

students made more references to source in the post-test 1, χ² (1) = 16.99, p < .001 (OR =

0.21, CI 0.07-0.61). However, there were no significant differences in the pre-test, χ² (1) =

0.14, p ≃ 1.00 (OR = 1.15, CI 0.38-3.49), and post-test 2, χ² (1) = 4.53, p = .10 (OR = 0.45,

CI 0.15-1.31). In addition, the interaction of group and condition, χ² (1) = 5.76, p = .02,

demonstrated the two groups did not differ in their references to the less reliable source, χ² (1)

= 0.91, p = .68 (OR = 0.72, CI 0.30-1.73), whereas trained students made more references to

the features of the more reliable source, χ² (1) = 11.73, p < .01 (OR = 0.31, CI 0.13-0.75).

Finally, the interaction between phase and condition, χ² (2) = 9.04, p < .05, indicated no

differences between the two sources in the pre-test, χ² (1) = 0.99, p = .96 (OR = 1.36, CI 0.56-

3.27), but differences were evident in both the post-test 1, χ² (1) = 7.62, p < .05 (OR = 2.28,

CI 0.97-5.32), and post-test 2, χ² (1) = 27.39, p < .001 (OR = 4.91, CI 2.06-11.68), with less

reference to the less reliable source after the intervention.

      Although the three-way interaction between group, phase and condition was not

significant, χ² (2) = 2.56, p = .28, the pattern of results suggests that trained students increased

their use of source information after the intervention and they did so specifically with the

more reliable as opposed to the less reliable source (see Figure 5). The increased reference to

source information in trained students was maintained three weeks later, showing again that

the intervention produced rather long-lasting effects.
disposition.calculation: No effect-size conversion or p-value transformation.

disposition.quote:
The

model demonstrated a significant main effect of group, χ² (1) = 10.68, p < .01, with more

correct responses in the trained (M = 0.72, SE ... = 0.15; OR = 0.39, CI 0.23-0.64); and phase, χ² (2) = 8.13, p < .05, with more correct

responses in the post-test 1 (M = 0.65, SE = 0.20) and post-test 2 (M = 0.71, SE = 0.21) than

in the pre-test (M = 0.52, SE = 0.19; OR = 0.52, CI 0.27-0.99 and OR = 0.42, CI 0.22-0.82 for

the post-test 1 and post-test 2, respectively). More importantly, the interaction between these

two factors was also significant, χ² (2) = 9.73, p < .01 (see Figure 4). Post-hoc comparisons

showed no group differences in the pre-test phase, χ² (1) = 0.0001, p ≃ 1.00 (OR = 0.99, CI

0.34-2.95); whereas the trained group outperformed the control group in the post-test 1, χ² (1)

= 14.90, p < .001 (OR = 0.19, CI 0.05-0.64), and post-test 2, χ² (1) = 7.19, p < .05 (OR = 0.31,

CI 0.09-1.08). Therefore, consistent with our hypothesis, trained students were better than

controls at detecting more reliable source information after the intervention. Importantly, this

finding was also true three weeks later, indicating the intervention had a rather robust impact. ... References to source in ... the post-test 1 (M = 0.47, SE = 0.17) and post-test 2 (M = 0.47, SE = 0.17) compared to the

pre-test (M = 0.24, SE = 0.19; OR = 0.33, CI 0.20-0.55 and OR = 0.34, CI 0.20-0.57 for the

post-test 1 and post-test 2, respectively); and condition, χ² (1) = 24.53, p < .001, with less

source reference to the less reliable (M = 0.29, SE = 0.16) compared to the more reliable

source (M = 0.49, SE = 0.15; OR = 2.48, CI 1.75-3.51).

      Importantly, the three two-way interactions were also significant. Post-hoc comparisons

in the interaction of group and phase, χ² (2) = 15.67, p < .001, demonstrated that trained

students made more references to source in the post-test 1, χ² (1) = 16.99, p < .001 (OR =

0.21, CI 0.07-0.61). However, there were no significant differences in the pre-test, χ² (1) =

0.14, p ≃ 1.00 (OR = 1.15, CI 0.38-3.49), and post-test 2, χ² (1) = 4.53, p = .10 (OR = 0.45,

CI 0.15-1.31). In addition, the interaction of group and condition, χ² (1) = 5.76, p = .02,

demonstrated the two groups did not differ in their references to the less reliable source, χ² (1)

= 0.91, p = .68 (OR = 0.72, CI 0.30-1.73), whereas trained students made more references to

the features of the more reliable source, χ² (1) = 11.73, p < .01 (OR = 0.31, CI 0.13-0.75).

Finally, the interaction between phase and condition, χ² (2) = 9.04, p < .05, indicated no

differences between the two sources in the pre-test, χ² (1) = 0.99, p = .96 (OR = 1.36, CI 0.56-

3.27), but differences were evident in both the post-test 1, χ² (1) = 7.62, p < .05 (OR = 2.28,

CI 0.97-5.32), and post-test 2, χ² (1) = 27.39, p < .001 (OR = 4.91, CI 2.06-11.68), with less

reference to the less reliable source after the intervention.

      Although the three-way interaction between group, phase and condition was not

significant, χ² (2) = 2.56, p = .28, the pattern of results suggests that trained students increased

their use of source information after the intervention and they did so specifically with the

more reliable as opposed to the less reliable source (see Figure 5). The increased reference to

source information in trained students was maintained three weeks later, showing again that

the intervention produced rather long-lasting effects.
disposition.calculation: No effect-size conversion or p-value transformation.

input.description: Article. The annotation covers OCs of (in)definite articles (a(n)/the). Given that the ‘zero article’ was disregarded in previous MOS, it was also disregarded here for comparative purposes. The non-suppliance of an article in an (in)definite OC was tagged as omission. Also, given that both definite and indefinite articles were analysed as a single morpheme in previous MOS, we analysed them similarly, even if we are aware that they are better analysed separately as they do not emerge simultaneously (cf. the discussion in Section 4.4). Selection of one article for the other was tagged as ‘mis-selection’. The forms a/an were understood as spelling variants, so selection of one when the other was expected was not tagged as NTLU. Importantly, determining the OC of the/a(n) is based on information-status distinctions deriving from discourse, i.e., on whether the entity has been previously mentioned in the discourse (i.e., discourse-old, topic) or not (i.e., discourse-new, focus), and therefore whether or not the referent is known to the reader. Articles were annotated independently of the appearance of characters in the picture story, which could give the sense of old information, but technically introduce discoursenew information when retelling the story to a reader. Therefore, ILA considers hearer/reader knowledge (and not speaker knowledge) to determine discourse-old/discourse-new distinctions (cf. Hawkins, 2001).

disposition.location: Materials and Methods, Study 5, canonical line 86; Results, Study 5, canonical line 49; SI referral line 65
disposition.quote: We addressed this possibility in preregistered study 5 by directly manipulating perceptions of AI either as a “black box” or as an explainable, nonmysterious system. We then asked participants to state their investment preference on a 101-point scale between two mutual funds, one recommended by a human and the other recommended by AI (0: strongly prefer algorithm, 100: strongly prefer human). The mysteriousness manipulation was successful; participants in the mysterious AI condition reported that it is significantly more uncertain to them how AI systems make decisions [Mmysterious AI = 4.91, SD = 1.63; Mnonmysterious AI = 3.10, SD = 1.50; F(1, 238) = 78.69, P < 0.001]. The main effect of the mysteriousness of the AI [F(1, 236) = 0.03, P > 0.8] and the interaction term [F(1, 236) = 0.006, P > 0.9] on the choice between the human and AI recommendations were insignificant. However, the main effect of God salience was significant [F(1, 236) = 9.25, P = 0.003]. Specifically, participants in the God salience condition exhibited a lower preference for the human recommendation (Mlow God salience = 55.61, SD = 17.12; Mhigh God salience = 47.74, SD = 22.48). This difference was significant both when the AI was a black box [Mlow God salience = 55.72, SD = 18.29; Mhigh God salience = 48.01, SD = 24.31; F(1, 236) = 4.89, P = 0.028] and when it was nonmysterious [Mlow God salience = 55.47, SD = 15.83; Mhigh God salience = 47.37, SD = 20.05; F(1, 236) = 4.41, P = 0.037]. ... Additional methodological information, sampling details, and full analyses are provided in SI Appendix. ... US-based participants (n = 281, Mage = 36.7 y, 167 female and 1 nonbinary) were recruited on Prolific in return for monetary payment.

blind.location: Appendix C, pp. 3, 5
blind.quote:
When we explored the results in the freshmen sample (the same restrictions used by

Lane et al.), the findings did not replicate the results of our entire sample or Lane et al.'s

results. Specifically, the explicit stereotype/attitudes relation (r = .157, p = .045) was not

significantly different from the IAT/explicit stereotype relation (r = .047, p = .550), Williams'

t(161) = 1.039, p = .300, and from the IAT/attitudes relation (r = .078, p = .322), Williams'

t(161) < 1, p = .463. Similarly, the IAT/importance relation (r = .143, p = .067) was not

significantly different from the explicit stereotype/importance relation (r = .113, p = .148),

Williams' t(161) < 1, p = .781, or the IAT/explicit stereotype relation, Williams' t(161) < 1, p

= .356. In the freshman sample, the IAT was not a better predictor of self-reported pursuit of

the topic stereotypically associated with the participant's gender (r = .111, p = .157) than the

explicit stereotype (r = .157, p = .045), Williams' t(161) < 1, p = .669. Because we replicated

Lane et al.'s results with the entire sample, we think that it is likely that the failure to replicate

the previous findings with a sample more similar to Lane et al.'s original sample reflects

random error, due to small sample size, rather than an actual limitation in the generalizability

of the previous findings.

disposition.reason: Authors distinguish replication in the entire sample from nonreplication in the freshmen sample. This narrative concerns predictive relations, and the assigned measure-only row does not identify that hypothesis or sample. No row-specific verdict assigned.

blind.location: Appendix C, pp. 3, 5
blind.quote:
When we explored the results in the freshmen sample (the same restrictions used by

Lane et al.), the findings did not replicate the results of our entire sample or Lane et al.'s

results. Specifically, the explicit stereotype/attitudes relation (r = .157, p = .045) was not

significantly different from the IAT/explicit stereotype relation (r = .047, p = .550), Williams'

t(161) = 1.039, p = .300, and from the IAT/attitudes relation (r = .078, p = .322), Williams'

t(161) < 1, p = .463. Similarly, the IAT/importance relation (r = .143, p = .067) was not

significantly different from the explicit stereotype/importance relation (r = .113, p = .148),

Williams' t(161) < 1, p = .781, or the IAT/explicit stereotype relation, Williams' t(161) < 1, p

= .356. In the freshman sample, the IAT was not a better predictor of self-reported pursuit of

the topic stereotypically associated with the participant's gender (r = .111, p = .157) than the

explicit stereotype (r = .157, p = .045), Williams' t(161) < 1, p = .669. Because we replicated

Lane et al.'s results with the entire sample, we think that it is likely that the failure to replicate

the previous findings with a sample more similar to Lane et al.'s original sample reflects

random error, due to small sample size, rather than an actual limitation in the generalizability

of the previous findings.

disposition.reason: Authors distinguish replication in the entire sample from nonreplication in the freshmen sample. This narrative concerns predictive relations, and the assigned measure-only row does not identify that hypothesis or sample. No row-specific verdict assigned.

t(161) < 1, p = .463. Similarly, the IAT/importance relation (r = .143, p = .067) was not

the topic stereotypically associated with the participant's gender (r = .111, p = .157) than the

explicit stereotype (r = .157, p = .045), Williams' t(161) < 1, p = .669. Because we replicated

Lane et al.'s results with the entire sample, we think that it is likely that the failure to replicate

random error, due to small sample size, rather than an actual limitation in the generalizability

of the previous findings.

disposition.quote:
Suppression-induced forgetting (lower memory performance for suppress compared with baseline items) was assessed using a mixed analysis of variance (ANOVA) with condition (baseline, suppress) as a within-subjects factor and group (PTSD, control) and set assignment (i.e., which of sets A, B, and C was assigned to each condition) as between-subject factors. Facilitation effects (better memory for recall compared with baseline items) were assessed using the same model, but the levels for condition were instead baseline and recall. disposition.quote:
Suppression-induced forgetting (lower memory performance for suppress compared with baseline items) was assessed using a mixed analysis of variance (ANOVA) with condition (baseline, suppress) as a within-subjects factor and group (PTSD, control) and set assignment (i.e., which of sets A, B, and C was assigned to each condition) as between-subject factors. Facilitation effects (better memory for recall compared with baseline items) were assessed using the same model, but the levels for condition were instead baseline and recall. ANOVAs were performed separately for each dependent measure (identification, gist, and details). ... Memory performance in the final test for the trauma-exposed control group (

(𝛽 = .094, 𝑝 < .05) positively impacted communication scholars’ intention toward data sharing, a finding
which differs from those reported by Harper and Kim (2018), who found no significant impacts on pressure
from open science journals or the availability of data repositories.
